Scale.0001.description:
Static content detected.

Your current approach of serving static content directly might lead to increased costs, performance issues, maintenance challenges (requiring application redeployment for content changes), and security risks.

Consider moving static content to Azure Blob Storage and adding Azure CDN.

Configuration.0003.description: Local application configuration detected. Azure App Configuration can be used as a centralized, cloud-based service for application settings that are currently stored in local configuration files. Moving this configuration to Azure App Configuration can help you externalize settings from code and deployment artifacts, centralize management across environments, and enable dynamic refresh and controlled access to configuration data.
Configuration.0003.title: Local application configuration detected

links.title: Configuration management with Azure App Configuration

Connection.0001.description:
Connection string detected. It may not be available when your app is migrated to Azure.

Review and ensure it works from Azure. If you are connecting to a database, you might need to migrate the database to Azure. There are multiple ways to do it:
    1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database for additional benefits (see the link below).
    2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
    3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.
Connection.0001.title: Connection string is detected

links.title: Migrate SQL Server database to Azure

Local.0003.description:
Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
    1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
    2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
    3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local.0003.title: Local or network IO operations detected

Database.0002.description:
SQL database connection detected.

Ensure the database is available/reachable on Azure.

If it is not, there are multiple ways you can move your data to Azure:
    1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database.
    2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
    3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.
Database.0002.title: SQL database connection detected

links.title: Migrate SQL Server database to Azure

Azure App Service provides built-in authentication and authorization capabilities, so you can sign in users and access data by writing minimal or no code in your web app.

Follow the link below for more information."

security.title: Unchecked Input for Loop Condition
security.description: The product does not properly check inputs that are used for loop conditions, potentially leading to a denial of service or other consequences because of excessive looping.

evidence.explanation: IndexModel.OnPostUploadAsync iterates over the caller-provided files collection without enforcing the configured MaxFilesPerUpload value. The number of per-file service operations is therefore controlled by the submitted multipart request; the request body has an overall limit but the individual loop count is not checked against the application limit.

security.title: Missing Release of Resource after Effective Lifetime
security.description: The product does not release a resource after its effective lifetime has ended, i.e., after the resource is no longer needed.

evidence.explanation: PhotoService.UploadPhotoAsync passes a newly opened IFormFile stream directly to Image.LoadAsync without disposing the stream. The subsequent OpenReadStream call at line 132 is also not disposed, leaving request stream wrappers unreleased after dimension extraction.

security.title: Use of Hard-coded Password
security.description: The product contains a hard-coded password, which it uses for its own inbound authentication or for outbound communication to external components.

evidence.explanation: The infrastructure template defines the SQL administrator password inline as a deterministic value derived from deployment identifiers and supplies it to the SQL server module. This embeds password construction in source rather than accepting a secret from a protected provisioning input.

security.title: Use of Hard-coded Credentials
security.description: The product contains hard-coded credentials, such as a password or cryptographic key.

evidence.explanation: The infrastructure template embeds construction of the SQL administrator credential in source and passes that value to the SQL server module, making a credential part of the deployed infrastructure definition.

security.title: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type
security.description: The product allows the upload or transfer of dangerous file types that are automatically processed within its environment.

evidence.explanation: PhotoService.UploadPhotoAsync accepts uploads based on the client-supplied ContentType allowlist, preserves the extension from the user-supplied filename, and writes bytes under the static web root. ImageSharp load failure is caught and upload continues, so content is not required to be a valid image. Program enables static file serving for the upload directory, allowing mismatched or active content with a permitted claimed MIME type to be stored and publicly served.

security.title: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
security.description: The product does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes user-controllable input before it is placed in output that is used as a web page that is served to other users.

evidence.explanation: PhotoService.UploadPhotoAsync trusts the client-supplied MIME type, preserves the uploaded filename extension, and continues after ImageSharp fails to decode the content. The file is saved below wwwroot, and Program enables static-file serving there. An attacker can upload HTML bytes while claiming an allowed image MIME type and using an .html extension; the static-file middleware can serve the uploaded content as an active same-origin HTML page.
